# About Accord Advisors

## Identity

Accord Advisors (rootadvisors.com) is a CPA firm with offices in Bloomington, Indiana (1516 South Walnut Street) and Avon, Indiana (7386 Business Center Drive, Suite B), serving the greater Indianapolis area and clients nationwide. The firm can be reached at 812-332-7200 or office@accordadvisors.com.

The firm's roots trace to Ally Accounting, founded in 2010 by Managing Partner Jared Hammack, a CPA since 2006 and Indiana University graduate who previously worked in international/complex tax at Deloitte. Ally Accounting grew through the acquisition of a local Indianapolis firm. Ryan Deckard also serves as Managing Partner. The team includes client managers, client accounting specialists, bookkeeping and payroll specialists, and administrative staff supporting day-to-day client service, including Kelly Root (Firm Administrator), Sean Hanthorn (Director of Operations), Jill Bailey, Amy Young, and Anita Altop (Client Managers), Wendi Elmore (Manager), Rachel Logston (Payroll Specialist), and others.

The firm is affiliated with the AICPA and the Indiana CPA Society. Its tone is approachable, trustworthy, reassuring, professional, supportive, and straightforward — blending accounting expertise with plain-language communication aimed at giving clients relief from financial burdens.

## Positioning & Differentiation

Accord Advisors positions itself as an outsourced accounting department and trusted advisor for business owners, medical and optometry practices, service businesses, churches, and individuals — supporting clients from startup through growth and succession. Rather than billing hourly, the firm charges fixed monthly fees and delivers services through a secure online platform.

Key differentiators include:
- Acting as an outsourced accounting department, providing CFO-level business management insight at a fraction of the cost of an in-house hire
- Fixed monthly fee pricing instead of hourly billing
- Deep industry-specific expertise, including nearly 40 years serving healthcare providers
- A secure online client platform
- Nationwide client reach from Indiana-based offices

Clients want to know how their business is performing each month and need relevant financial and non-financial data and dashboards to make informed decisions — a need the firm addresses through its outsourced accounting and reporting services. Optometry clients are frequently referred through Acquios (acquios.com).

## Industries Served

### Optometry Practices
Accord Advisors provides specialized accounting support for optometry practices and their retail optics operations. Pain point: managing growth and profitability across combined clinical and retail optics operations. Value proposition: industry-specific accounting support tailored to the dual clinical/retail nature of optometry practices.

### Medical Professionals
With nearly 40 years of experience, the firm provides tax, accounting, and payroll services for healthcare providers. Pain points: cost management and reimbursement challenges. Value proposition: long-tenured, healthcare-specific expertise across tax, accounting, and payroll.

### Dental Practices
The firm offers tax, accounting, and payroll services for dental practices and providers. Pain points: cost management and reimbursement challenges, similar to other healthcare providers. Value proposition: dedicated tax, accounting, and payroll support built around the financial realities of dental practices.

### Service Businesses
Accord Advisors provides back-office financial support and strategic planning for attorneys, law firms, and consulting companies. Value proposition: outsourced back-office accounting and strategic planning support for professional service firms.

### Churches
The firm provides fund accounting and financial stewardship support for churches. Pain points: staffing and compliance challenges. Value proposition: specialized fund accounting expertise to help churches maintain financial stewardship and meet compliance requirements despite staffing constraints.

## About RootAdvisors your trusted accounting partner

### Nearly 40 years of accounting experience
URL: /team-expertise

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: accountant-reviewing-documents-office.jpg | alt: "CPA reviewing financial documents in a Bloomington Indiana office" | query: "accountant reviewing documents office" -->
## A firm built on decades of local accounting expertise

Nearly 40 years is a long time to spend in one profession, in one region. RootAdvisors has been doing the books, filing the returns, and answering the tough questions for Bloomington and Indianapolis business owners since long before cloud accounting existed. Jared Hammack, CPA, leads a firm that grew up alongside the businesses it serves, not one that parachuted in from a national office to sell a template.

That history matters. National firms rotate staff, standardize advice, and bill by the hour for every phone call. A firm rooted in central Indiana for four decades knows which local banks move fastest on a loan, which industries are hiring, and which tax rules actually apply to a dentist in Bloomington versus a service contractor in Indianapolis. Clients don't get a stranger every renewal season. They get the same advisor, year after year, who already knows their business before the meeting starts.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: optometry-dental-practice-review.jpg | alt: "Optometrist and accountant reviewing practice financial reports together" | query: "optometrist accountant reviewing reports" -->
## Deep experience with optometry and dental practices

Optometry and dental practices run on numbers most CPAs never learn: capitation rates, insurance panel mixes, associate buy-in structures, and equipment depreciation schedules that stretch a decade or more. RootAdvisors has worked through those numbers with practice owners for close to 40 years, long enough to spot a staffing cost creeping out of line before it becomes a crisis.

Many optometry clients arrive through [Acquios](https://acquios.com/), the industry referral network connecting practice managers with accountants who already speak the language of OD practices. That's not a coincidence. Understanding [practice management metrics](/industries/optometry/practice-management-metrics), from patient volume to exam-chair utilization, takes repetition, not a crash course. [Dentists](/industries/dentists) face a parallel set of challenges: hygienist payroll, lab fees, and multi-location scheduling. Decades in both fields means fewer surprises and faster answers when a practice owner calls with a question that can't wait for a scheduled meeting.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: physician-financial-review.jpg | alt: "Physician reviewing financial statements with an accountant" | query: "physician reviewing financial statements" -->
## Trusted by medical professionals and healthcare providers

Healthcare reimbursement does not sit still. Payer mixes shift, coding rules change, and cash flow can swing hard between a slow claims month and a catch-up payment. Physicians, physician assistants, and other [medical professionals](/industries/medical-professionals) who bring their books to RootAdvisors get an advisor who has watched these patterns play out across nearly four decades of practices in Bloomington and Indianapolis.

That experience shows up in specifics: knowing which [reimbursement challenges](/industries/medical-professionals/reimbursement-challenges) tend to hit primary care differently than a specialty practice, or recognizing when a slow quarter is seasonal rather than a warning sign. Jared Hammack, CPA, and the RootAdvisors team use that pattern recognition to help healthcare providers plan cash flow around the realities of medical billing, not a generic small-business model.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: service-business-owner-planning.jpg | alt: "Service business owner reviewing growth plans with an accountant" | query: "business owner meeting accountant planning" -->
## Experience supporting service businesses through every stage

Service businesses rarely stay the same shape for long. A two-person shop becomes a ten-person operation, then starts thinking about fleet vehicles, equipment financing, or a succession plan for the owner who built it. RootAdvisors has guided [service-based clients](/industries/service-businesses) across Bloomington and Indianapolis through each of those stages, from the first year of incorporation through the day an owner hands off the business.

That range of experience means startup questions get the same seasoned attention as a succession plan. An owner adding a second truck or a fleet of vans benefits from [fleet and equipment planning](/industries/service-businesses/fleet-and-equipment-planning) grounded in real depreciation schedules, not guesswork. An owner nearing retirement gets a team that has already walked other clients through a [sale or an internal transition](/services/succession-planning), because that work has been part of the practice for years.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: church-finance-meeting.jpg | alt: "Church administrator reviewing financial reports with an accountant" | query: "church administrator financial meeting" -->
## A long history of guiding churches and religious organizations

Church finances follow their own rules: designated funds, stewardship reporting to a congregation instead of shareholders, staffing structures that mix pastoral roles with lay employees, and compliance requirements unique to religious nonprofits. RootAdvisors has worked with [churches and religious organizations](/industries/churches) in and around Bloomington long enough to know these are not edge cases. They are a core part of the practice.

That means fewer generic nonprofit templates and more direct answers about [staffing and compliance](/industries/churches/staffing-and-compliance) for an administrator trying to keep payroll correct for both W-2 staff and clergy with special tax treatment. It also means practical guidance on [fraud prevention](/fraud-prevention-strategies-for-nonprofit-organizations), since limited financial oversight is a real risk for many congregations. Decades in this niche translate into faster, more specific answers than a firm encountering church accounting for the first time.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Why decades of experience matter more than hourly billing

Experience only helps a client if it doesn't cost more every time the phone rings. RootAdvisors pairs its history with a [fixed monthly fee for outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting), so a Bloomington business owner never has to hesitate before asking a question or wonder what a fifteen-minute call is about to cost.

That structure works because the experience is already there. A firm still learning an industry needs more billable hours to reach the right answer. A firm that has handled optometry practices, medical offices, service businesses, and churches for close to 40 years gets there faster, and passes that efficiency along as a predictable monthly cost instead of a variable invoice. Add a secure online platform for sharing documents and reviewing financials, and clients get CFO-level insight without CFO-level overhead. [Business foundation services](/services/business-foundation-services), from entity setup to bookkeeping systems, are built on the same fixed-fee approach from day one.

### Personal income tax preparation and planning
URL: /services/personal-income-tax

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Personal tax help that goes beyond filing a return

For most people, taxes are a once-a-year scramble: gather the documents, drop them off somewhere, sign what you're handed, and hope for the best. That works fine if your financial life is simple. It works less well if you own a practice, run a service business, or make decisions today that carry tax consequences three years from now.

Accord Advisors treats personal income tax preparation as a year-round relationship, not a spring transaction. Clients in Bloomington and Indianapolis bring us questions in July about a home sale, in October about a retirement account, in January about a bonus. We're already thinking about next year's return while we finish this year's. That's a different posture than a seasonal storefront preparer can offer, and it's the one we take with every individual client on our books.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: personal-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Advisor and client reviewing personal tax documents at a desk" | query: "financial advisor client meeting documents" -->
## Who we help with personal tax planning

Most of our individual tax clients aren't purely individuals. They're business owners, optometry practice shareholders, physicians, dentists, and service business operators who also need someone thinking about their household return. A lot of firms split that work: one preparer for the business, another for the personal return, neither talking to the other.

We don't split it. The same advisor who handles your [practice's outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) or [business foundation services](/services/business-foundation-services) also prepares your personal return, because your K-1, your distributions, and your retirement contributions all flow through one financial picture. Optometrists and [medical professionals](/industries/medical-professionals) referred to us through their industry networks tell us this coordination is the piece they were missing before.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: tax-planning-checklist-review.jpg | alt: "CPA pointing to a tax planning checklist with a client" | query: "accountant explaining tax documents client" -->
## What our personal tax preparation and planning includes

A personal return prepared once a year, without context, is a guess dressed up as accuracy. Ours starts earlier and covers more ground:

- Accurate, complete preparation of federal and Indiana state returns, reviewed by a CPA before filing
- Proactive tax planning throughout the year, not a single meeting in March
- Guidance around major life events: retirement distributions, sale of a practice, [succession planning](/services/succession-planning), or a business sale that changes your tax picture
- Estimated payment calculations so you're never guessing what to send the IRS quarterly
- Coordination with your business accounting so personal and business tax strategy don't work against each other
- Plain-language explanations of what changed on your return and why, before you ever sign it

The goal is simple: no surprises in April, and no scrambling to reconstruct a year's worth of decisions in the two weeks before the deadline.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: secure-client-portal-laptop.jpg | alt: "Client uploading tax documents through a secure online portal on a laptop" | query: "person using laptop online document upload" -->
## Fixed fees and a secure client experience

Hourly billing turns every phone call and every question into a math problem. Wondering whether it's worth calling your accountant shouldn't be part of tax planning. That's why Accord Advisors prices personal tax preparation and planning as a fixed monthly or annual fee, agreed to upfront, so you know the cost before the work starts and can call as often as you need without a meter running.

Documents move through a secure online client portal instead of email attachments or a folder of paper dropped off at a front desk. Upload a W-2, a 1099, or a closing statement whenever it arrives, and it's there for us to work with immediately. No physical files sitting in a car, no faxing, no waiting for an office to reopen.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: business-owner-tax-strategy-discussion.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA discussing tax strategy documents together" | query: "business owner accountant discussing strategy" -->
## Why business owners choose RootAdvisors for personal tax

Owners who run a practice or a service business have a personal return that's rarely simple. Distributions, retirement plan contributions, entity structure, and depreciation choices on the business side all land on the personal return eventually. Handling those separately from two different firms invites gaps.

Jared Hammack, CPA, leads tax planning for individuals alongside the firm's outsourced accounting and business foundation clients, which means the same advisor who sees your monthly financials also prepares your 1040. That's CFO-level insight applied to a personal return, not just data entry at tax time. Visit [team expertise](/team-expertise) to see the credentials behind that advice, or read [why RootAdvisors](/why-rootadvisors) works differently from a typical local preparer.

### Business foundation services for new practice owners
URL: /services/business-foundation-services

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: new-practice-owner-planning.jpg | alt: "New optometry practice owner reviewing paperwork with an advisor" | query: "new business owner meeting advisor office" -->
## Starting a practice is exciting, but the paperwork can be overwhelming

Opening an optometry practice, dental office, medical clinic, or service business means juggling patient care or client work alongside decisions you never trained for: entity formation, tax elections, payroll setup, banking, state registrations. Most new owners figure it out by trial and error, which is exactly how expensive mistakes get baked into year one. Jared Hammack, CPA, has guided new practice owners through this stage for nearly 40 years, working closely with optometrists and healthcare providers across Bloomington and Indianapolis. You don't need to become an accountant overnight. You need someone who has solved these problems hundreds of times already and can tell you, plainly, what matters now and what can wait until next quarter.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Choosing the right entity structure from day one

The entity you choose in your first 90 days, S-corp, LLC, professional corporation, sets the tax treatment and liability protection your practice lives with for years. Change it later and you're often looking at additional filings, transition costs, and sometimes a higher tax bill than if you'd started right. Optometrists and dentists face particular nuances: Indiana professional licensing rules affect which entity types are even available, and payroll tax treatment differs sharply between an S-corp salary and a sole proprietor draw. Jared Hammack, CPA, walks new owners through the real trade-offs before anything is filed with the state, comparing self-employment tax exposure, reasonable compensation requirements, and liability separation side by side. The goal isn't the textbook answer. It's the structure that fits your practice, your growth plans, and how you actually want to pay yourself in year one and year five.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: bookkeeping-setup-healthcare-practice.jpg | alt: "Accountant setting up bookkeeping software for a new healthcare practice" | query: "accountant reviewing financial software office" -->
## Setting up accounting systems built for your practice

From your first week seeing patients or clients, you need to know how the practice is actually performing, not guess at it three months later when the tax return is due. RootAdvisors builds your chart of accounts and bookkeeping system around how optometry, dental, and medical billing actually work: insurance reimbursements, patient copays, vendor terms for frames or supplies, and multiple revenue streams that generic software lumps together into one line. Everything runs through a secure online platform, so you and your practice manager can check real numbers anytime, not just when someone remembers to ask. New owners tell us the same thing: nobody explained, before RootAdvisors, how their bank balance connected to what they were actually earning. That gap closes in the first 30 days, not the first tax season.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: compliance-checklist-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing a compliance checklist with financial documents" | query: "business owner reviewing compliance documents" -->
## Navigating licensing, registrations, and compliance basics

Between opening day and your first quarter close, a dozen registration and compliance deadlines can quietly pass you by: state tax ID, employer withholding registration, local business licensing, workers' comp, sales tax if you sell retail products like frames or supplies. Miss one and the penalty shows up months later, disconnected from the original mistake. RootAdvisors keeps a launch checklist specific to Indiana requirements and works through it with you line by line, before you're too busy running the practice day to day to notice a gap.

- Federal EIN and Indiana state tax ID registration
- Indiana Department of Revenue withholding and sales tax accounts
- Local business registration in Bloomington or Indianapolis
- Payroll setup, including employer tax deposits and W-2/1099 tracking
- Workers' compensation and unemployment insurance coordination
- Professional licensing renewal calendars for optometry, dental, and medical practices

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Planning your fixed monthly investment as you grow

Hourly billing punishes you for asking questions, and the startup phase is exactly when you have the most questions. RootAdvisors works on a fixed monthly fee instead, set based on your practice's size and complexity, not the clock. You can call about a vendor contract, a hiring decision, or a tax notice without watching a meter run. That predictability matters most in year one, when cash flow is tightest and every dollar needs a plan. As your practice grows, the fixed fee adjusts to match added complexity, but it never surprises you. You get CFO-level insight into your numbers at a fraction of what a full-time controller or an hourly-billed firm would cost.

### IRS notice protection and response support
URL: /services/irs-notice-protection

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Getting an IRS letter doesn't have to mean panic

A letter from the IRS lands in the mail and the first reaction is almost always dread. For an optometrist juggling patient schedules, a dentist managing staff payroll, or a church treasurer trying to keep the books straight, an IRS notice feels like an emergency dropped on an already full plate.

Most notices are routine. A mismatched 1099, a payroll tax discrepancy, a question about a deduction. Jared Hammack, CPA, and the team at RootAdvisors read these letters every week for clients across Bloomington and Indianapolis, Indiana. You don't have to figure out what it means or what to say back. Bring it to us first, and we'll tell you exactly what's going on and what happens next.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: vertical -->
## What we handle for you when a notice arrives

### We read the notice line by line

Every IRS letter has a notice number, a deadline, and a specific ask buried in the language. We identify exactly what the IRS wants, why they're asking, and whether it's a simple clarification or something that needs a documented response.

### We check it against your actual records

Before we respond to anything, we compare the notice to your filed returns, payroll records, or bookkeeping data. Sometimes the IRS has bad information. Sometimes a filing slipped through the cracks. Either way, we find the truth before we act on it.

### We communicate directly with the IRS

With proper authorization, we contact the IRS on your behalf, by phone or in writing, so you're not the one sitting on hold or trying to decode agency language.

### We draft and file the response

We prepare the documentation, write the response, and submit it by the deadline. You review it, you approve it, and it's handled. You never face the IRS alone on this.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: irs-notice-review-desk.jpg | alt: "CPA reviewing an IRS notice letter alongside client financial documents at a desk" | query: "accountant reviewing official letter documents" -->
## Common notices we help Bloomington and Indianapolis clients resolve

Optometry practices, dental offices, medical providers, service businesses, and churches all tend to run into a handful of recurring IRS notices. We've handled these repeatedly for clients across Indiana:

- Income reporting mismatches, when a 1099 or W-2 filed by a payer doesn't match what shows up on your return
- Payroll tax discrepancies, common in practices with multiple staff, contractors, or shift-based employees
- Notices about estimated tax underpayment for practice owners and shareholders
- Missed or late filings flagged after a busy season or a staffing gap in the office
- Questions about deductions claimed for equipment, vehicles, or church-related expenses
- Requests for additional documentation to support a return already filed

None of these mean you did something wrong. Most mean the IRS needs a clearer picture, and that's exactly what we provide.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: fixed-fee-consultation.jpg | alt: "Advisor and client reviewing a flat fee service agreement together" | query: "advisor client reviewing agreement office" -->
## Why our fixed-fee approach removes the fear of surprise costs

Stress about an IRS letter is bad enough without also wondering what the phone call to your accountant is going to cost. Firms that bill by the hour turn a fifteen-minute question into a line item, and clients hesitate to call until the deadline is already close.

RootAdvisors works on a flat monthly fee. If you're already a client, notice support is part of the relationship, not a separate invoice that grows with every email. If you're new to us, we quote the work up front before we start, so you know the cost before you commit to anything. That certainty matters most exactly when you're least in the mood to gamble on a bill.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: healthcare-practice-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA consulting with an optometry practice manager in a clinical office setting" | query: "consultant meeting healthcare practice manager" -->

RootAdvisors has served healthcare providers for nearly 40 years, working closely with optometry practices, dental offices, and medical professionals across Bloomington and Indianapolis, Indiana. Jared Hammack, CPA, has sat across from practice managers dealing with payroll notices tied to hygienist or associate optometrist compensation, and church treasurers navigating clergy housing allowance questions. That history means fewer surprises. We've usually seen your specific notice before, for a client very much like you.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: bookkeeping-records-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant organizing monthly bookkeeping records and tax documents" | query: "organized financial records bookkeeping" -->

Our [Outsourced Accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) service keeps your books current every month, so income and payroll figures match what actually happened in your practice or business. ## Payroll support built for growing teams

Payroll gets more complicated the moment you add a second provider, a new associate optometrist, or a part-time hygienist. Tax withholdings change, filing deadlines multiply, and one missed deposit can trigger a penalty notice you didn't see coming. For optometry practices, dental offices, medical clinics, service businesses, and churches across Bloomington, Indianapolis, and Avon, payroll administration from RootAdvisors removes that burden from your plate.

We run payroll as part of a full [outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) department, not as a bolt-on service handled by a call center. Jared Hammack, CPA, and the team behind RootAdvisors have spent close to 40 years working inside healthcare practices and small businesses, so payroll decisions get made with your books, your tax return, and your growth plans in view, not in isolation. Every pay run, filing, and deposit runs on a fixed monthly fee, through a secure online platform you can check anytime. No hourly surprises. <!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: payroll-processing-review.jpg | alt: "Office manager reviewing payroll reports on a laptop" | query: "office manager reviewing payroll laptop" -->
## What our payroll administration covers

Payroll administration sounds simple until you're the one running it between patient appointments or job sites. Here's what we take off your desk each pay period:

- Processing payroll on your schedule, weekly, biweekly, or semi-monthly
- Calculating federal, state, and local tax withholdings correctly
- Filing quarterly and annual payroll tax returns on time
- Setting up and managing direct deposit for every employee
- Onboarding new hires, including tax forms and state new-hire reporting
- Preparing year-end W-2s and 1099s for staff and contractors

Each task connects back to your general ledger and tax return automatically, so nothing gets re-entered or reconciled twice by you or your practice manager.

Everything runs through a secure online platform where you and your practice manager can see pay history, filings, and reports whenever you need them, not just when the payroll company emails a PDF. ### Succession planning for business owners
URL: /services/succession-planning

<!-- block: hero-split | variant: image-right -->

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: business-owner-planning-transition.jpg | alt: "Business owner and accountant reviewing succession planning documents at a desk" | query: "business owner advisor planning meeting" -->
## Plan your business transition with confidence

Selling a business, retiring, or handing the reins to a family member rarely happens in a single moment. It's a sequence of financial decisions made months, sometimes years, before the actual transition. Wait too long and you risk a lower sale price, a tax bill that eats into your retirement, or a handoff that leaves employees and clients unsettled.

Succession planning gives you a roadmap instead of a scramble. RootAdvisors works through the numbers early: what your business is worth today, what it could be worth with cleaner financial reporting, and what a buyer, partner, or successor will actually want to see. Jared Hammack, CPA, and the team build that groundwork inside your existing outsourced accounting relationship, so the reporting you already rely on becomes the same data that supports a well-documented exit.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: indiana-small-business-meeting.jpg | alt: "Small business owners meeting with financial advisor in a conference room" | query: "small business meeting financial planning" -->
## Why succession planning matters for local business owners

Business owners in Bloomington and across the Indianapolis area often put succession planning off until a health scare, an unsolicited offer, or a family disagreement forces the issue. By then, options narrow considerably.

Waiting carries specific costs:

- A valuation gap that surfaces only after a buyer's due diligence team finds incomplete or inconsistent financial records
- Capital gains and estate tax exposure that could have been reduced with structuring done two or three years earlier
- Family or partner disputes over ownership percentages, compensation, or timing that stall a transition indefinitely
- Client or patient relationships that erode during a rushed, poorly communicated handoff

Indiana practices and service businesses that start the conversation five to ten years before a planned exit generally negotiate from a position of strength, not urgency.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: vertical -->
## Our approach to succession readiness

### Financial statement cleanup
We review your books for accuracy and consistency, correcting anything that would raise questions during a sale, merger, or ownership transfer. Clean, consistent financials are the foundation every later step depends on.

### Cash flow analysis
Buyers and successors want to see predictable cash flow, not just revenue. We isolate owner perks, one-time expenses, and seasonal swings so the true earning power of the business is visible.

### Business structure review
Your entity type, ownership agreements, and compensation arrangements affect both tax outcomes and transferability. We flag structural issues while there is still time to fix them.

### Valuation readiness
We prepare the financial documentation a buyer, bank, or family successor will request, reducing the back-and-forth that stalls deals and lowers offers.

### Transition roadmap
You get a written timeline tied to your fixed monthly fee, covering tax positioning, reporting cleanup, and the milestones that need to happen before closing.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: optometry-practice-succession.jpg | alt: "Optometrist reviewing practice transition documents with an accountant" | query: "optometrist consulting accountant office" -->
## Succession planning for optometry and dental practices

Transitioning an optometry or dental practice carries a layer of complexity most business sales don't. Patient records have to move in compliance with state and federal privacy rules. Associate buy-ins need a valuation method both the departing owner and incoming partner trust. A practice's value is tied closely to patient retention, payer mix, and equipment age, factors a generic business appraisal often misses.

RootAdvisors has worked inside healthcare financial reporting for nearly 40 years, and that background shapes how we prepare a practice for sale or internal transfer. We help structure associate buy-in terms, model the cash flow impact of a phased retirement, and organize the financial statements that optometry and dental buyers, including groups referred through platforms like Acquios, expect to see before making an offer.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: church-service-business-leadership.jpg | alt: "Church finance committee and service business owner in a planning meeting" | query: "nonprofit church finance meeting" -->
## Succession planning for service businesses and churches

Service businesses and religious organizations face a different kind of succession problem: leadership transition often matters as much as ownership transfer. A contracting or consulting firm needs financial continuity when a founder steps back, including documented processes for billing, payroll, and vendor relationships that don't live in one person's head.

Churches and religious organizations face their own version of this challenge when a longtime administrator, treasurer, or pastor with financial oversight moves on. We help boards and finance committees document giving records, reserve policies, and reporting practices so continuity survives a leadership change, not just an ownership one.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How we work with your attorney and financial advisors

Succession planning touches legal documents, estate planning, and sometimes insurance, areas outside a CPA's scope. RootAdvisors doesn't try to replace your attorney or financial advisor. We handle the financial data those professionals need: clean statements, cash flow projections, valuation-ready reports, and tax modeling for whatever transaction structure they recommend.

That division of labor keeps the process efficient. Your attorney drafts the buy-sell agreement or trust. Your financial advisor addresses your personal retirement income. RootAdvisors makes sure the numbers behind both are accurate and current, delivered through the same secure online platform you already use for outsourced accounting, so nothing gets lost between advisors.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: bloomington-business-handshake.jpg | alt: "Two business owners shaking hands after a planning meeting" | query: "business owners handshake agreement" -->
## Start your succession conversation today

Succession planning works best when it starts early and stays simple. If you're a Bloomington or Indianapolis business owner thinking about retirement, sale, or a generational handoff in the next few years, the financial groundwork should start now, not at closing. Schedule a consultation with RootAdvisors and we'll walk through where your business stands today and what a well-prepared transition would require, backed by a fixed monthly fee, no hourly surprises, and a CPA-led team that already knows healthcare, service business, and church finances.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: optometry-inventory-pressures.jpg | alt: "Optical frames and lenses displayed on shelves in an optometry office" | query: "optometry office frame inventory display" -->
## Understanding the financial pressures optometry practices face

Optometry is a retail business and a medical practice running side by side, and that combination creates pressure points that don't show up in a standard CPA's playbook.

- Frame and lens inventory that ties up working capital and needs regular turnover analysis, not a once-a-year count
- Insurance reimbursement timing that leaves gaps between the exam and the cash actually landing in your account
- Staffing costs that swing with patient volume, from opticians and technicians to front-desk coverage
- Owner compensation questions that get tangled up with the practice's real profitability
- The need for monthly, not annual, visibility into how the practice actually performed

Without monthly clarity, staffing and purchasing decisions get made on instinct instead of numbers. That's an expensive way to run a practice.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: outsourced-accounting-optometry.jpg | alt: "Accountant working on secure online platform with optometry practice financials" | query: "accountant laptop financial reports office" -->
## Outsourced accounting designed for your practice

Most optometry practices don't need a part-time bookkeeper and a separate CPA for taxes stitched together and hoped for the best. They need one accounting relationship that covers both, billed at a clear monthly rate instead of a running hourly meter.

Our [Outsourced Accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) service functions as your practice's full accounting department: bookkeeping, financial statements, payroll coordination, and CFO-level insight, delivered for a fixed monthly fee agreed on before work begins. No surprise invoice after a phone call to ask a question. You also get a secure online platform where you can review your practice's financials any time, from any location, instead of waiting on a printed report or a buried email attachment.

For a two-location practice, or a single office competing against a regional optical chain, that combination of dependable monthly reporting and a fixed cost changes how you plan. You know what accounting will cost in July and in December. Your numbers stay current when a lender, a potential partner, or an incoming associate optometrist asks to see them.

## Personal and business tax planning under one roof

For most service business owners, personal and business taxes aren't separate problems. They're the same problem viewed from two angles. A pass-through entity's business income lands on your personal return, and a decision made in December about equipment or compensation changes what you owe in April.

RootAdvisors handles [personal income tax preparation and planning](/services/personal-income-tax) alongside your business accounting, so the same team that reviews your monthly financials is also planning your personal return. That coordination catches things a once-a-year tax preparer misses: estimated payments that need adjusting, retirement contributions that reduce this year's liability, or an entity election that changes your effective tax rate.

Owners of consulting firms, law practices, and other service businesses in Bloomington and Indianapolis get one team handling both sides of the return, instead of reconciling advice from two firms that never talk to each other.

<!-- block: stats-bar | variant: 3-up -->

RootAdvisors has advised Indiana business owners for nearly 40 years, with roots in Bloomington and a growing base of clients in Indianapolis. That history means a service business here gets an accountant who already understands Indiana filing requirements, local business registration rules, and how a college-town client roster differs from one built around a state capital market. See [why Indiana business owners choose RootAdvisors](/why-rootadvisors).

- Nearly 40 years advising Indiana business owners
- 2 core markets served: Bloomington and Indianapolis
- 100% fixed-fee engagements, no hourly billing

A national firm files paperwork. A local one knows why your client roster looks different in August than it does in January.

### Fund accounting for churches
URL: /industries/churches

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Trusted fund accounting for churches and religious organizations

Ministry leadership shouldn't have to guess whether the building fund is on track or whether restricted mission gifts are being spent the way donors intended. Accord Advisors has worked alongside churches and religious organizations in Bloomington and the surrounding Indiana communities, bringing fund accounting expertise that goes beyond basic bookkeeping. Jared Hammack, CPA, leads this work with an approach built on clarity: your board sees exactly how funds move, your treasurer isn't buried in spreadsheets, and your congregation's trust stays intact.

Fund accounting exists to protect stewardship, not just satisfy an audit checklist. When a church tracks a mission trip fund, a building campaign, and general operating income the same way it tracks a single checking account, restricted dollars get muddled with unrestricted ones, and leadership loses the ability to answer a simple question: how did we do this month? That's the gap we close, with reporting built specifically for how churches operate.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: church-finance-meeting.jpg | alt: "Church treasurer and pastor reviewing financial reports together at a table" | query: "church staff financial meeting" -->
## Why churches need specialized fund accounting

Standard small-business bookkeeping tracks one bottom line: profit. Churches operate differently. A single congregation might manage a general operating fund, a designated missions fund, a building or capital campaign fund, and a benevolence fund, each with its own restrictions on how and when the money can be spent. Mixing them together in a generic chart of accounts creates confusion at best and a compliance problem at worst.

Fund accounting separates every dollar by its designated purpose and reports on each fund independently, while still rolling up into a clear picture of overall financial health. That distinction matters when a donor gives specifically toward a youth ministry scholarship or a roof repair. Your board and finance committee need to know, every month, whether restricted funds are being used as intended and whether unrestricted giving is covering operating costs. Without that clarity, even well-meaning church leaders can misallocate funds without realizing it. Getting this structure right from the start protects both the ministry's integrity and the trust of the people who give to it.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: bookkeeper-church-office.jpg | alt: "Accountant working on church bookkeeping records at a laptop" | query: "bookkeeper working office laptop" -->
## Outsourced accounting built for churches

Most churches don't need, or can't afford, a full-time controller. Accord Advisors fills that role as an outsourced accounting department, handling the fund tracking, bookkeeping, payroll coordination, and monthly financial statement preparation that keep a church's books accurate and current. Everything runs through a secure online platform, so your treasurer, pastor, or finance committee chair can log in and see up-to-date numbers instead of waiting on a spreadsheet emailed once a quarter.

The engagement runs on a fixed monthly fee, not hourly billing. That means a church finance committee can budget for accounting support the same way it budgets for utilities or staffing, with no surprise invoice after a busy giving season or year-end audit prep. It also means the relationship is built around ongoing support rather than one-off transactions: fund reconciliations get done every month, restricted gifts get coded correctly as they come in, and reports are ready well before your board meeting, not scrambled together the night before.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: board-meeting-review.jpg | alt: "Church board members reviewing printed financial statements during a meeting" | query: "nonprofit board meeting documents" -->
## Financial statements and reporting your board can trust

A church board or elder team shouldn't need an accounting background to understand where the money stands. Accord Advisors prepares fund-based financial statements that separate restricted and unrestricted balances clearly, so a treasurer can walk into a monthly meeting and answer questions with confidence instead of guesswork.

- Monthly fund balance reports showing restricted vs. unrestricted activity
- Statements formatted for board and elder review, not accountant jargon
- Year-over-year comparisons to track giving trends and expense patterns
- Documentation ready for annual audits or denominational reporting requirements
- Direct access to reports through a secure online platform, anytime a question comes up

When leadership can see performance clearly each month, decisions about staffing, building projects, or ministry expansion get made with real data behind them, not a rough guess based on the checking account balance.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: new-church-setup-finance.jpg | alt: "Pastor and financial advisor setting up new accounting system on a computer" | query: "small church office setup planning" -->
## Getting your church's financial foundation right

A growing congregation or a newly organized church often inherits an accounting setup that was never built for fund tracking in the first place, maybe a generic small-business chart of accounts, or a spreadsheet a volunteer built years ago. Accord Advisors' Business Foundation Services address that directly: establishing a proper fund-based chart of accounts, setting up internal controls around cash handling and disbursement approval, and structuring designated funds so they're tracked correctly from day one.

This matters as much for a five-year-old church plant as it does for an established congregation adding a new building fund or launching a benevolence ministry. Weak internal controls, even in a trusted, well-run church, create risk: unclear approval processes, no separation of duties around who counts offering and who deposits it, no documented policy for how restricted gifts get recorded. Getting the foundation right the first time means fewer corrections later, cleaner audits, and a finance committee that isn't rebuilding its books every time a new treasurer takes over.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Tax and compliance support for religious organizations

Churches face a set of tax and compliance questions that don't come up in typical small-business accounting: clergy housing allowance calculations, dual tax status for ministers who are employees for income tax but self-employed for Social Security and Medicare, proper W-2 versus 1099 treatment for church staff, and the nonprofit filing requirements that come with 501(c)(3) or church-exempt status.

Getting clergy compensation wrong is one of the most common, and costly, mistakes a church makes. Housing allowances have to be designated in advance and documented correctly, and payroll has to reflect the minister's dual tax status accurately or the church risks penalties down the line. Accord Advisors works through these details directly with church treasurers and finance committees, so payroll runs correctly, compensation is documented the way the IRS expects, and any required nonprofit filings get handled on schedule. The goal is straightforward: your church stays compliant, and your staff and volunteers spend their time on ministry, not tax research.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: church-community-support.jpg | alt: "Church leaders shaking hands after a financial planning conversation" | query: "church leaders handshake meeting" -->
## Partner with a CPA firm that understands ministry

A church's finances should support its mission, not distract from it. Accord Advisors works with congregations across Bloomington and the Indianapolis area to bring fund accounting clarity, dependable monthly reporting, and compliance support that lets treasurers, elders, and pastors focus on the work in front of them. Jared Hammack, CPA, and the team are ready to talk through where your church's accounting stands today and what a fixed monthly outsourced relationship could look like.

[Schedule a consultation](/contact) to start the conversation.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: dental-office-front-desk-billing.jpg | alt: "Dental office front desk staff processing insurance billing paperwork" | query: "dental office front desk billing" -->
## Challenges unique to running a dental office

Dental practices operate on a rhythm most CPAs never see up close: daily production numbers, insurance write-offs, and hygiene department goals that shift month to month. Without a system built for that rhythm, it's easy to lose track of what a practice actually earned last month versus what got billed.

Insurance reimbursements complicate the picture further. Claims get delayed, adjusted, or denied, and reconciling what was collected against what was produced takes a bookkeeper who understands dental fee schedules, not just general ledgers.

Add staffing costs, hygienist pay structures, and equipment financing, and most owners end up reviewing financials weeks after the month has closed, if at all. RootAdvisors builds reporting around the numbers that matter to a dental office: production, collections, overhead ratios, and staffing costs, delivered on a schedule that lets you make decisions while they still matter.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: dental-practice-financial-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Financial dashboard reports for a dental practice on a tablet screen" | query: "financial dashboard tablet office" -->

Outsourced accounting from RootAdvisors covers the full back office of a dental practice, not just tax time. Bookkeeping stays current so production and collections numbers are ready the moment you want them, not weeks later.

Monthly reporting turns raw numbers into dashboards built for the decisions dentists actually make: adding a hygienist, financing new equipment, or evaluating whether it's time to bring on an associate.

- Monthly bookkeeping reconciled against production and collections reports
- Payroll support for dental staff, associates, and hygienists
- Financial statements delivered on a predictable monthly schedule
- Dashboards showing overhead ratios and cash flow trends
- Secure online access to reports and documents anytime

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: dentist-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Dentist and CPA reviewing tax planning documents at a desk" | query: "tax planning meeting dentist accountant" -->
## Tax preparation and planning for dentists

Dental practice tax returns rarely stay simple. Entity structure, associate buy-ins, equipment purchases, and retirement plan contributions all shift the tax picture year to year, and preparation without planning tends to cost owners money.

Jared Hammack, CPA, and the RootAdvisors team review entity structure, whether you operate as an S corp, LLC, or professional corporation, to confirm it still fits your practice's income and goals. Section 179 deductions on dental equipment, retirement plan strategy for owners and associates, and quarterly estimates get built into a year-round plan rather than a once-a-year filing.

Personal returns for practice owners and associates get the same attention, so business and personal tax positions stay aligned instead of working against each other.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: new-dental-practice-setup.jpg | alt: "New dental practice owner setting up office with contractor" | query: "new dental practice setup owner" -->

## Find the right forms for your industry and stage

Every business owner has hit the same wall: searching for a tax form, or wondering what a new accountant actually needs before they'll start work. This page exists to save you that search.

Jared Hammack, CPA, and the RootAdvisors team have spent close to 40 years refining these lists for healthcare providers, churches, and growing businesses across Bloomington and Indianapolis. ## New client onboarding and outsourced accounting documents

Moving your books onto RootAdvisors' outsourced accounting platform starts with a short list of documents, not a mountain of paperwork. Most new clients have these ready within a week:

- Prior year business tax returns and financial statements
- Bank and credit card statements for the last 12 months
- Payroll records and current payroll provider information
- Vendor and accounts payable list
- Entity documents, such as articles of incorporation, an operating agreement, or bylaws
- Signed engagement letter outlining scope and your fixed monthly fee
- Login setup for our secure online client portal

Once those are on file, your engagement letter locks in one fixed monthly fee, no hourly billing surprises, and you're active on the secure portal where you can upload documents, review financials, and message your accounting team directly. See how the full process works on our [outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) page.

## Tax forms and resources for medical, dental, and optometry practices

Healthcare practices carry accounting complexity that a generic small-business checklist won't cover: equipment depreciation schedules, insurance reimbursement reports, associate compensation structures, and multi-provider payroll. We've built practice-specific document lists for optometry, dental, and medical clients so nothing gets missed at tax time.

For optometrists, that typically includes practice financial statements, equipment purchase and depreciation records, associate doctor 1099s or W-2s, and vision plan reimbursement summaries. ## Accounting resources for service businesses and churches

Service businesses and churches share one thing in common: revenue that doesn't move in a straight line. Contractors bill by job. Consultants bill by retainer. Churches rely on contributions that swing with the calendar and the congregation.

For service businesses, our resource list covers vendor W-9 collection templates, expense and mileage tracking forms, and job costing worksheets that feed directly into your monthly financials. For churches and religious organizations, we provide contribution tracking templates, restricted fund logs, and staffing compliance checklists that keep payroll and benefits reporting in order.

Both sets of resources are built to plug into an outsourced accounting engagement, so the data you collect becomes the dashboard you actually use to make decisions. ## Business foundation checklists for startups and growing companies

Starting a business, or restructuring one that's outgrown its original setup, comes with a specific stack of paperwork. Our Business Foundation Services clients typically work through this checklist first:

- Entity formation and EIN application documents
- Operating agreement or corporate bylaws
- Bookkeeping system setup and chart of accounts
- State and local business registration filings
- Payroll registration with state and federal agencies
- Sales tax permit applications, where applicable
- Initial budget and cash flow projections

We walk founders through each item in order so nothing gets filed out of sequence or missed entirely. If you're past startup and into growth mode, the same checklist doubles as a health check, showing which foundational pieces might need a second look. Learn more about how [business foundation services](/services/business-foundation-services) fit into your timeline.

## Personal income tax preparation checklist

Personal tax prep shouldn't require a background in accounting to get right. Here's what most individual clients need to gather before their appointment:

- W-2s and 1099s from all employers or clients
- Mortgage interest and property tax statements
- Records of charitable contributions
- Documentation for dependents and childcare expenses
- Prior year tax return, if you're new to RootAdvisors
- Records of any self-employment or rental income

Bring what you have. If something's missing, we'll tell you exactly what to track down instead of pointing you back to a generic list. Our [personal income tax](/services/personal-income-tax) page has more detail if you want to look ahead.

## Send documents securely

Tax returns, payroll records, and financial statements contain information you don't want floating through unsecured email. Our secure file transfer option encrypts documents from the moment you upload them until our team opens them, so sensitive data stays protected at every step.

Use this option whenever you need to send:

- W-2s, 1099s, and other tax forms
- Bank and credit card statements
- Payroll records or employee data
- Signed engagement letters or authorization forms
- Practice or business financial reports

### Post
URL: /resources-new/post

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why this topic matters to local business owners

Every optometry practice, dental office, and service business we work with in Bloomington and Indianapolis asks a version of the same question at some point: how did we actually do last month? Not gut feeling, not a bank balance glance, but real numbers that show whether the practice grew, stalled, or quietly bled cash on supplies and payroll.

Owners running a Monroe County practice or a growing service business in Indianapolis rarely have time to build that clarity themselves. Between patient care, staffing, and the daily fires that come with running a business, the monthly dashboard gets skipped. That gap is where good decisions turn into guesses, and it's the exact gap this post is built to close.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: financial-dashboard-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing monthly financial dashboard on laptop screen" | query: "business owner reviewing financial report laptop" -->
## What the numbers are telling you

A monthly financial dashboard is a short, plain-language snapshot: revenue against last month and last year, gross margin by service line, cash on hand, days in accounts receivable, and payroll as a percentage of revenue. For an optometry practice, that might mean tracking exam volume against eyewear sales. For a service business, it might mean labor cost per job.

The point isn't the spreadsheet. It's the pattern. A dip in gross margin two months running usually means supply costs crept up or pricing hasn't kept pace with inflation. A steady rise in accounts receivable days often signals a billing or collections problem before it shows up as a cash crunch.

Most owners we talk to in Bloomington have some of this data buried in their bookkeeping software. Almost none of them have it organized into something they can read in five minutes and act on. That's the difference between having numbers and having answers, and it's why dashboards matter more than raw reports.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: reviewing-practice-financials.jpg | alt: "Practice manager and accountant reviewing printed financial statements together" | query: "accountant client reviewing financial statements" -->
## Common mistakes practices and businesses make

We see the same handful of missteps across optometry, dental, medical, service business, and church clients:

- **Reviewing financials once a quarter, or once a year at tax time.** By the time a problem shows up in the annual numbers, three or four months of decisions have already been made on bad information.
- **Tracking revenue without tracking margin.** An optometry practice can grow top-line revenue while gross margin quietly shrinks because frame costs or lab fees rose without a corresponding fee adjustment.
- **Treating payroll as a fixed cost instead of a percentage of revenue.** Dental and medical practices with hygienists, techs, and front-office staff often don't notice payroll creeping past a healthy range until cash gets tight.
- **Letting accounts receivable age without a clear collections process,** especially common in service businesses billing on invoice terms and in medical practices waiting on insurance reimbursement.
- **Church finance teams relying on a single volunteer bookkeeper** with no second set of eyes on monthly giving trends or restricted fund tracking.

None of these mistakes are about effort. They're about not having the right numbers organized the right way, on a schedule that matches how fast the business actually moves.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cpa-team-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA advisor discussing financial strategy with small business client in office" | query: "cpa advisor meeting small business client" -->
## How outsourced accounting solves this

This is exactly the gap our [outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) work is built to close. Instead of billing by the hour for whatever question comes up, we handle the bookkeeping, reconciliations, and monthly reporting for a fixed monthly fee, so a Bloomington optometry practice or an Indianapolis service business always knows what the relationship costs before the month starts.

Jared Hammack, CPA, has spent close to four decades working with healthcare providers, which means the dashboards we build for an optometry or dental client reflect how those practices actually operate, not a generic template pulled from a general business account. Data lives on a secure online platform, so a practice manager can log in and see current numbers rather than waiting on an emailed spreadsheet.

For businesses still getting the basics in place, [Business Foundation Services](/services/business-foundation-services) sets up the chart of accounts, systems, and processes that make accurate monthly reporting possible in the first place. Get the foundation right, and the dashboard becomes a five-minute read instead of a monthly scramble.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: bloomington-office-consultation.jpg | alt: "Accountant and client shaking hands after a consultation meeting" | query: "handshake consultation office meeting" -->
## Next steps for your practice or business

You don't need to overhaul your entire accounting system to start getting clearer answers. A good starting point is simply pulling last month's numbers and asking whether you can explain, in one sentence, why revenue or margin moved the way it did. If you can't, that's worth a conversation.

We work with optometry practices, dental offices, medical professionals, service businesses, and churches across Bloomington and Indianapolis, and most conversations start with a look at what you're already tracking and where the gaps are. No pressure, no long sales process, just a straightforward look at your numbers with someone who's spent years in healthcare and small business accounting.

[Schedule a consultation](/contact) and let's look at what your monthly numbers should be telling you.

### Zero based budgeting a smarter way to manage your money during persistent inflation
URL: /zero-based-budgeting-a-smarter-way-to-manage-your-money-during-persistent-inflation

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why traditional budgets break down when prices keep rising

Most budgets start with last year's numbers and add a percentage for inflation. That worked fine when prices moved two percent a year. It stops working when a bag of exam-room supplies costs 18% more than it did in 2021, or when a hygienist's starting wage has climbed four dollars an hour since your last budget cycle.

Practice owners and service business owners across Bloomington and Indianapolis are finding that last year's budget, adjusted upward, no longer reflects what things actually cost today. Rent renewals, payroll, insurance premiums, and vendor contracts have all moved independently of each other, and a flat percentage bump doesn't capture any of it.

Zero-based budgeting throws out the assumption that last year's numbers are a fair starting point. Every dollar gets justified from zero, every month, based on what your business actually needs right now. For a CPA firm working with optometry practices, dental offices, and service businesses managing rising costs on multiple fronts, that distinction matters.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: zero-based-budget-planning.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing monthly budget spreadsheet on a laptop" | query: "small business owner reviewing budget laptop" -->
## How zero based budgeting works for your business or household

Zero-based budgeting flips the traditional approach. Instead of starting with what you spent last year and adjusting it up or down, you start every month at zero and build the budget from scratch, dollar by dollar, based on what the business actually needs during that period.

For a practice owner, that means asking real questions each month. Does the office need a new round of exam supplies, or is inventory already stocked? Is a locum covering vacation time this month, adding a temporary labor cost? Is there a seasonal marketing push planned? Every expense has to earn its place in the budget instead of coasting in because it was there last year.

The same logic applies at home. Rather than assuming last year's grocery or utility number still holds, every dollar of income gets assigned a specific job before the month begins: rent, savings, debt payoff, discretionary spending.

The result is a budget that reflects what's actually happening in a business or household right now, not what happened twelve months ago when supply costs and wages looked different.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Why this approach matters most for optometry and dental practices, medical professionals, and service businesses

Practice managers and shareholders tell us the same thing: they want to know how the business performed this month, not just at tax time. Zero-based budgeting feeds that need directly, because it forces a fresh look at costs and revenue every single month instead of once a year.

### Optometry and Dental Practices
icon: Stethoscope

Frame costs, lab fees, and staffing needs shift monthly depending on patient volume and case mix. Building the budget from zero each month gives practice managers and shareholders a real-time view of margin instead of a guess based on last year's schedule.

### Medical Professionals
icon: HeartPulse

Reimbursement rates change, staffing needs fluctuate with patient volume, and supply costs move independently of revenue. A zero-based approach keeps the budget tied to what's happening in the practice this month, not a projection built a year ago.

### Service Businesses
icon: Briefcase

Job costs, subcontractor rates, and material prices move throughout the year. Rebuilding the budget from zero each month keeps pricing and profitability decisions grounded in current numbers instead of outdated assumptions.

### Churches
icon: Building2

Giving patterns shift with the seasons, and building maintenance or program costs rarely move in a straight line. Zero-based budgeting gives treasurers and finance committees a month-by-month picture that matches actual giving and actual need.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: reviewing-financial-records.jpg | alt: "Accountant pointing out figures on a financial statement to a client" | query: "accountant reviewing financial statement with client" -->
## Common mistakes local business owners make when they try this alone

Zero-based budgeting sounds simple in theory: start at zero, justify every dollar. In practice, business owners who try it without clean books underneath run into the same problems.

- Building the budget on numbers that are already out of date, because bookkeeping is two or three months behind
- Mixing personal and business expenses, which makes it impossible to tell what a category actually costs
- Skipping the monthly rebuild after the first cycle, so the zero-based budget quietly turns back into last year's budget
- Working without a consistent chart of accounts, so this month's numbers can't be compared to last month's
- Treating it as a once-a-year project instead of a recurring, month-by-month discipline

Every one of these mistakes traces back to the same root cause: the underlying financials weren't accurate or current enough to build a real budget on top of them.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cpa-client-monthly-review.jpg | alt: "CPA and business owner reviewing monthly accounting reports on a tablet" | query: "CPA client meeting reviewing reports tablet" -->
## How RootAdvisors builds zero based budgeting into your monthly financial process

Zero-based budgeting only works if the numbers underneath it are accurate and current. That piece gets built first, through outsourced accounting that keeps books closed and reconciled every month, not three months behind.

Once the foundation is solid, the budget conversation gets real. Instead of hourly billing that makes every phone call feel like a cost, Accord Advisors works on a fixed monthly fee, so a practice manager or business owner can ask questions about a spending category without watching the clock.

A secure online platform gives clients access to current financial data whenever they want it, rather than waiting for a quarterly meeting. Business Foundation Services set up the chart of accounts, close process, and reporting structure a zero-based budget depends on, so the monthly rebuild is based on real numbers instead of estimates.

Jared Hammack, CPA, has spent close to four decades working with healthcare providers and service businesses on exactly this kind of financial infrastructure, building budgets that hold up when costs keep moving.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: bloomington-indiana-office-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA and business owner shaking hands after a consultation meeting" | query: "business owner CPA handshake consultation" -->
## Getting started with a smarter budget in Bloomington and Indianapolis

Persistent inflation isn't going away on its own, and a budget built on last year's numbers won't tell you what's really happening in your practice or business this month. Zero-based budgeting works when it's built on accurate, current books, updated every month, by someone who understands healthcare and service-business finances specifically.

Accord Advisors serves optometry practices, dental offices, medical professionals, service businesses, and churches throughout Bloomington and Indianapolis. Schedule a consultation to talk through what a zero-based budget would look like for your specific numbers, with no hourly clock running while you ask questions.
