### Upskilling your workforce a smart strategy for overcoming labor market shortages
URL: /upskilling-your-workforce-a-smart-strategy-for-overcoming-labor-market-shortages

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why labor shortages are pushing employers toward upskilling

Finding qualified staff in Bloomington and across the Indianapolis area has gotten harder, not easier. Optometry practices need trained technicians who can run new diagnostic equipment. Dental offices need hygienists and front-desk staff who understand insurance billing. Medical practices, service businesses, and churches are all competing for the same shrinking pool of skilled workers.

Hiring from outside costs more than most owners expect once recruiting fees, onboarding time, and lost productivity get added up. Training the staff already on your payroll is often the more affordable path forward, and it carries a benefit many employers overlook: money spent on employee education and skills training can reduce your tax bill. Understanding how those training costs flow through your books is where the real savings show up.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How workforce training expenses affect your business taxes

The federal tax code generally treats employee training as an ordinary and necessary business expense, the same category as rent or office supplies. Continuing education for licensed staff, software and equipment training, safety certifications, and skills courses tied to an employee's current position typically qualify for a deduction in the year you pay for them.

The line gets blurrier when training prepares an employee for a different job or profession rather than improving performance in the one they already hold. That distinction matters more than most business owners realize, and getting it wrong can mean missing a deduction you're entitled to or claiming one you shouldn't.

This is general information, not tax advice for your specific situation. Every practice and business has different facts, and the right treatment depends on what the training covers, who receives it, and how it's documented. That's a conversation worth having before tax season, not during it.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: indiana-workforce-training-resources.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing state workforce development program materials at desk" | query: "business owner reviewing paperwork office" -->
## Indiana resources and credits that support employee development

Indiana offers more support for workforce training than many employers realize. The Indiana Department of Workforce Development runs programs and grant opportunities designed to help employers train new and existing staff, and state lawmakers have periodically discussed expanding tax incentives tied to workforce credentialing.

Knowing these programs exist is one thing. Applying them correctly to your specific practice or business, and making sure the numbers land where they should on your tax return, is another. We help Bloomington and Indianapolis-area business owners figure out which state programs actually apply to their situation, then make sure the accounting reflects it accurately so nothing gets left on the table at filing time.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: clinical-staff-training-session.jpg | alt: "Dental hygienist training a new team member on sterilization equipment" | query: "medical staff training clinical setting" -->
## What this means for optometry, dental, and medical practices

Clinical staffing is its own puzzle. [Optometry](/industries/optometry) practices need opticians and technicians who can handle new equipment and evolving insurance requirements. [Dental](/industries/dentists) offices depend on hygienists and assistants trained on current sterilization and billing standards. [Medical](/industries/medical-professionals) practices face similar pressure with clinical staff and front-desk teams who manage scheduling, coding, and patient intake.

Training an existing employee to take on a higher-skill role, cross-training front-desk staff on billing software, or funding a technician's certification renewal are all costs that typically qualify for deduction, provided they're documented and tied to the employee's current position. Practices that track these expenses correctly get two wins: a more capable team and a cleaner tax return.

We work with optometry, dental, and medical practices across Bloomington and Indianapolis to make sure training costs are categorized correctly from the start, not reconstructed at year-end.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: service-business-team-training.jpg | alt: "Service business owner training staff on new equipment in workshop" | query: "trade worker training equipment shop" -->
## What this means for service businesses and churches

Service businesses face a different version of the same problem: skilled trades and technical roles that take months to fill from outside. Training current employees on new equipment, safety protocols, or licensing requirements is often faster and cheaper than hiring, and the costs are typically deductible when properly documented.

Churches carry an added layer. Paid staff training, such as bookkeeping software instruction for an office administrator or safety training for facilities staff, is generally treated like any other business expense. Volunteer training is different and usually isn't deductible the same way, which makes clear recordkeeping between paid and volunteer roles essential.

Getting the distinction right protects a church's tax-exempt status and keeps the books audit-ready. Learn more about staffing considerations for [churches](/industries/churches) or explore support for [service businesses](/industries/service-businesses).

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: outsourced-accounting-dashboard-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing financial dashboard on laptop with client remotely" | query: "accountant reviewing financial dashboard laptop" -->
## How outsourced accounting keeps your training investment tax-ready

Training expenses only produce a tax benefit if they're captured correctly throughout the year, not reconstructed from receipts in April. [Outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) through RootAdvisors tracks these costs as they happen, for a fixed monthly fee, through a secure online platform you can check anytime.

- Training and certification costs coded correctly the month they're paid
- Clear separation between deductible staff training and non-deductible personal education
- Monthly financial reporting that shows the real cost of your training investment
- CFO-level insight into whether upskilling or hiring makes more financial sense for your next role
- A tax return built on a full year of accurate records, not a scramble in March

Practices and businesses building strong internal systems from the ground up often start with our [business foundation services](/services/business-foundation-services) before layering in ongoing accounting support.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: bloomington-cpa-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA advisor shaking hands with business owner in bright office" | query: "cpa advisor meeting business owner" -->

### Fraud prevention strategies for nonprofit organizations
URL: /fraud-prevention-strategies-for-nonprofit-organizations

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: nonprofit-board-meeting-review.jpg | alt: "Nonprofit board members reviewing financial documents together at a table" | query: "nonprofit board meeting financial review" -->
## Why churches and nonprofits are common fraud targets

Nonprofits and churches run lean. A single bookkeeper often handles deposits, disbursements, and reconciliations because the budget doesn't support a full accounting team. That concentration of duties, combined with a culture built on trust rather than suspicion, creates exactly the conditions fraud examiners warn about.

The Association of Certified Fraud Examiners has found nonprofit organizations lose a median of $75,000 per fraud case, often absorbed by an organization that can least afford it. Volunteers handle cash offerings on Sunday mornings. Small staffs mean the same person who opens the mail also records the deposit and reconciles the bank statement. Board members, often volunteers themselves, may not have the accounting background needed to spot irregularities in a financial statement.

Bloomington and Indianapolis-area nonprofits face this reality without the internal audit departments larger organizations rely on. That's where practical, right-sized controls make the difference.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: bookkeeper-reviewing-receipts.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeper reviewing receipts and invoices at a desk" | query: "bookkeeper reviewing receipts office" -->
## Warning signs of internal fraud in nonprofit organizations

Fraud rarely announces itself. It shows up in small inconsistencies that get explained away until they can't be anymore. Board members and church leaders in Bloomington should treat these signs as reasons to look closer, not as one-off mistakes.

- Bank or credit card statements that go unreconciled for more than a month
- Missing receipts, invoices, or documentation for reimbursements
- One person controlling deposits, disbursements, and recordkeeping with no second signature
- Vendors or payees the board doesn't recognize
- A staff member or volunteer reluctant to take vacation or hand off duties
- Financial reports that arrive late, inconsistent, or without detail
- Donor or contribution records that don't match bank deposits

Any one of these might have an innocent explanation. Several together, especially around cash handling or reconciliations, warrant a closer look from someone outside day-to-day operations.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->
## Core internal controls every nonprofit should have

Fraud prevention isn't about distrust. It's about structure. These four controls form the foundation of [Business Foundation Services](/services/business-foundation-services) for churches and nonprofits, and they cost far less to put in place than a single embezzlement case costs to absorb.

### Segregation of duties
icon: Users

No single person should open mail, make deposits, record transactions, and reconcile the bank statement. Splitting these tasks across two or more people, even in a five-person office, closes the gap most embezzlement schemes exploit.

### Dual approval on payments
icon: ShieldCheck

Checks and electronic payments above a set threshold require a second signature or approval. This one step stops the majority of check-tampering and unauthorized disbursement schemes before money leaves the account.

### Monthly reconciliations
icon: FileCheck

Bank and credit card statements get reconciled every month, not whenever there's time. Discrepancies get caught within weeks instead of surfacing a year later during an audit.

### Board-level financial oversight
icon: ClipboardCheck

Someone outside daily operations, typically a treasurer or finance committee, reviews financial statements each month and asks questions about anything that doesn't look right.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: outsourced-accounting-team-review.jpg | alt: "Accounting team members reviewing financial reports on a computer screen" | query: "accounting team reviewing reports office" -->
## How outsourced accounting strengthens fraud protection

Handing bookkeeping to one internal employee, however trusted, still leaves a single point of failure. RootAdvisors' [outsourced accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) model splits the work across a team: one person handles data entry, another reviews and reconciles, and a CPA reviews the financials before they reach the board. That separation exists automatically, without hiring additional staff.

Every transaction runs through a secure online platform where church and nonprofit leaders can see activity in real time rather than waiting for a year-end audit to find a problem. Fixed monthly fees mean there's no incentive to skip reconciliations or shortcut a review to save billable hours, a risk that comes built into hourly-billed engagements.

Jared Hammack, CPA, has spent close to 40 years working with healthcare providers, service businesses, and nonprofit organizations across Bloomington and Indianapolis, and has seen firsthand how thin staffing turns good intentions into open doors for fraud. Outsourcing the accounting function doesn't just save time. It rebuilds the checks and balances a two-person office can't provide on its own.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: financial-dashboard-laptop-review.jpg | alt: "Nonprofit leader reviewing financial dashboard on a laptop screen" | query: "person reviewing financial dashboard laptop" -->
## Financial dashboards and reporting that catch problems early

Boards and church councils can't act on numbers they don't see. RootAdvisors provides monthly financial reporting built around the questions leadership actually asks: how did the organization perform this month, are expenses tracking where expected, and does contribution income match what came in through the offering plate or online giving platform.

Dashboards flag variances as they happen rather than months later. A vendor payment that doesn't match a prior pattern, a reimbursement that spikes unexpectedly, or a reconciliation that won't balance shows up in the reporting a board member reviews each month, not in a forensic accountant's report after the money is gone.

That kind of visibility does double duty. It supports fraud prevention, and it gives boards the operational insight they need to make informed decisions about programs, staffing, and giving trends throughout the year.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Building a fraud prevention plan with a Bloomington CPA firm

Every nonprofit and church is different: different staff size, different cash handling needs, different board structure. A fraud prevention plan has to fit the organization, not a generic template downloaded from the internet.

RootAdvisors has worked with Bloomington and Indianapolis-area [churches](/industries/churches), service organizations, and nonprofits for close to 40 years, building controls that match how small and mid-size organizations actually operate. That means practical recommendations: which duties to split when there are only three staff members, how often a treasurer should review statements, what documentation a volunteer-run finance committee needs to keep. Learn more about how RootAdvisors supports [church staffing and compliance](/industries/churches/staffing-and-compliance) needs alongside fraud prevention.

The goal isn't a binder that sits on a shelf. It's a set of controls the organization can actually maintain, backed by outsourced accounting support that keeps the checks and balances running month after month rather than reviewed once a year and forgotten. Meet the CPA behind this work on the [team expertise](/team-expertise) page.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: cpa-consultation-handshake.jpg | alt: "CPA shaking hands with nonprofit leader after a consultation meeting" | query: "handshake business consultation meeting" -->

### Selling a business rental or large asset this year call your CPA before you sign
URL: /selling-a-business-rental-or-large-asset-this-year-call-your-cpa-before-you-sign

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why timing your call matters more than the sale price

Most of the real tax planning on a sale happens before you sign anything, not after. Installment sale elections, cost segregation reviews, entity restructuring, and gain deferral strategies all depend on decisions made while the deal is still a draft. Once ink hits paper, the IRS treats the transaction as done, and so do most of the planning options that would have reduced your tax bill.

We see this most often with optometrists selling a practice, dentists retiring out of a group, service business owners entertaining a buyout offer, and landlords negotiating the sale of a rental property in Bloomington or Indianapolis. The sale price matters. What matters more is what you keep after taxes, and that number gets decided weeks or months before closing, not at the closing table.

A short conversation with a CPA before you sign can change the structure of the deal itself, not just the paperwork around it.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: business-sale-consultation.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA reviewing a purchase agreement together at a desk" | query: "business owner meeting accountant documents" -->
## Common transactions that need advance tax planning

Every sale looks different depending on the entity, the asset, and the buyer. A few scenarios come up often with our clients:

- An optometrist selling a practice to an associate or a group, where goodwill allocation and non-compete payments change the tax treatment of nearly every dollar
- A dentist retiring and transferring equipment, chairs, and instruments, where depreciation recapture can turn a routine handoff into a surprise tax bill
- A service business owner exiting through an asset sale or stock sale, where the choice between the two changes who pays what and when
- A landlord selling a rental building, where depreciation recapture and 1031 exchange timelines have hard deadlines that do not bend
- A church disposing of property, where unrelated business income rules and use restrictions require a different kind of review entirely

Each of these needs its own strategy. None of them benefit from a generic answer worked out after the fact.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## What can go wrong when you sign first and call later

The damage from skipping pre-sale planning is rarely dramatic. It shows up quietly, as a bigger tax bill than expected or a planning option that closed the moment the contract was executed.

An installment sale election, for example, has to be built into how the deal is structured, not applied afterward. Miss that window and a seller who could have spread a gain over several years owes it all in one. Depreciation recapture on equipment or real estate is calculated based on what was claimed over the years the asset was owned, and there is no way to undo that exposure once the sale closes. Capital gains treatment can shift dramatically depending on how a purchase agreement allocates the price between goodwill, equipment, and real property, a detail buyers and sellers often negotiate without anyone flagging the tax consequence.

None of this means a deal is doomed if you have not called us yet. It means the earlier the call happens, the more options are still on the table.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cpa-pre-sale-planning-session.jpg | alt: "CPA and client discussing financial documents during a planning meeting" | query: "accountant client planning session office" -->
## How RootAdvisors helps you plan before you sign

RootAdvisors works as an outsourced accounting department for optometry practices, dental practices, medical professionals, service businesses, and churches across Bloomington and Indianapolis, and pre-sale planning is where that ongoing relationship pays off. Jared Hammack, CPA, has spent close to 40 years working with healthcare providers on exactly these transactions, from practice sales to equipment transfers to retirement transitions.

Because we bill a fixed monthly fee instead of the hour, a pre-sale planning conversation does not come with the anxiety of a surprise invoice. You call, we talk through the structure, and we tell you what the numbers look like before you commit to anything. Documents move back and forth through a secure online platform, so purchase agreements, depreciation schedules, and appraisals stay organized and accessible to everyone who needs them, without email attachments floating around.

The goal is simple: you know the tax consequence of a deal before you are legally bound to it.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-right | image: sale-documents-review.jpg | alt: "Folder of financial documents and depreciation schedules on a desk" | query: "financial documents folder desk review" -->
## What to bring to your pre-sale consultation

The first meeting goes faster, and further, when you bring the numbers with you. For most sellers, that means:

- Any draft purchase agreement or letter of intent, even an early one
- Current depreciation schedules for the business, equipment, or property involved
- Original purchase price and improvements made to the asset since acquisition
- Recent financial statements or tax returns for the business or rental activity
- A rough timeline for the sale, including any deadlines the buyer has proposed

You do not need a finished deal or a signed contract to have this conversation. A term sheet, a verbal offer, or even a serious inquiry from a buyer is enough to start the planning work.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: bloomington-cpa-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA advisor shaking hands with a business owner in a Bloomington office" | query: "handshake advisor client office meeting" -->
## Talk to a CPA in Bloomington or Indianapolis before you sign anything

If you are an optometrist, dentist, medical professional, service business owner, or church leader weighing a sale this year, the best time to call is before the paperwork is final, not after. RootAdvisors works with clients across Bloomington and Indianapolis on exactly these transactions, and a short conversation now can shape the structure of a deal that has not closed yet.

Schedule a consultation before you sign, and bring whatever paperwork you have. We will tell you what we see.

### When and why every business owner needs a business valuation
URL: /when-and-why-every-business-owner-needs-a-business-valuation

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why guessing your business's worth puts your future at risk

Most business owners carry a number in their head. It might come from a competitor's sale price, a comment a banker made at a chamber event, or a formula pulled off the internet. That number rarely holds up when it matters most.

For optometry practices, dental offices, medical groups, service businesses, and churches across Bloomington, Avon, and Indianapolis, the gap between a gut-feel estimate and an actual valuation becomes expensive fast. It shows up during a partner buyout negotiation, a succession plan, or a bank's request for collateral documentation. By then, there's no time to build the case properly. A real valuation, done ahead of the moment you need it, closes that gap before it costs you.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: business-valuation-meeting.jpg | alt: "Business owner and advisor reviewing valuation documents at a desk" | query: "business owner reviewing financial documents advisor" -->
## Key moments that trigger the need for a valuation

A valuation isn't a once-in-a-lifetime document you pull out only when you're ready to sell. Certain moments make it a requirement, not an option:

- Succession planning, when a practice owner is preparing to hand the reins to a family member, associate, or management team
- Partner buy-ins or buyouts, where a fair, defensible number protects every party at the table
- Bringing on a new physician, optometrist, dentist, or associate who will eventually hold equity
- Divorce proceedings, where a business interest must be valued accurately for the settlement
- Estate planning, so heirs and trustees know the true value of what they're inheriting
- Preparing to sell an optometry, dental, medical, or service practice to an outside buyer or private equity group

Each of these situations puts real money on the table. A valuation grounded in your actual financials, not a rule of thumb, gives you a number you can stand behind in a negotiation, a courtroom, or a bank meeting.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: valuation-analysis-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant analyzing practice financial statements and growth trends" | query: "accountant analyzing financial statements office" -->
## The real insight a valuation delivers for your practice

A valuation produces a dollar figure, but the number is the least useful part for owners who plan to keep running the business. The process behind it surfaces what's actually working and what isn't.

A thorough valuation examines your revenue trends, patient or client retention, staffing costs, payer mix, and cash flow patterns. It flags operational risks a monthly bookkeeping report never would, like over-reliance on a single referral source or thin margins hiding behind strong top-line revenue. For a practice manager trying to decide whether to bring on an associate or invest in new equipment, that operational detail matters more than the headline valuation figure. It's the kind of insight that turns a static financial statement into a decision-making tool.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: optometry-dental-practice-consult.jpg | alt: "Optometrist and advisor discussing practice financial performance" | query: "optometrist dentist consultation office setting" -->
## Why healthcare and service business valuations require specialized expertise

A generalist valuation approach treats every business the same: revenue multiple, adjust for owner compensation, done. That method misses the details that actually drive value in a healthcare or service business.

Accord Advisors has worked with optometry, dental, and medical practices for nearly 40 years. Jared Hammack, CPA, and the team understand how payer contracts, associate compensation structures, and equipment depreciation schedules affect what a practice is genuinely worth, not just what a spreadsheet formula suggests. Service businesses and churches carry their own nuances too: fleet and equipment costs, staffing compliance requirements, and revenue patterns that don't look like a typical retail or manufacturing business. That specificity changes the outcome. Explore how this expertise applies to [optometry practices](/industries/optometry), [dental practices](/industries/dentists), [medical professionals](/industries/medical-professionals), [service businesses](/industries/service-businesses), and [churches](/industries/churches).

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: clean-financial-records-review.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeper organizing monthly financial statements and ledgers" | query: "bookkeeper organizing financial records office" -->
## How outsourced accounting sets the foundation for an accurate valuation

A valuation is only as strong as the financial records behind it. Messy books, inconsistent categorization, or six months of catch-up bookkeeping slow the process down and drive up the cost of getting it done right.

Accord Advisors' [Outsourced Accounting](/services/outsourced-accounting) services keep your monthly financials clean, consistent, and ready whenever a valuation, sale, or succession conversation comes up. Pair that with [Business Foundation Services](/services/business-foundation-services), and you've got the entity structure, chart of accounts, and reporting discipline that a valuation professional needs from day one instead of scrambling to reconstruct later. Owners who build this foundation early move faster and pay less when the valuation moment actually arrives, whether that's a planned exit or an unplanned life event.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: bloomington-advisor-consultation.jpg | alt: "Advisor and business owner shaking hands after a consultation meeting" | query: "advisor client handshake consultation meeting" -->
## Getting started with a valuation conversation

A valuation doesn't have to wait for a crisis, and it doesn't have to feel intimidating. Whether you're an optometry practice manager thinking about succession, a service business owner fielding an unsolicited offer, or a church board planning for the future, the right time to start the conversation is before you need the answer.

### Transfer pricing and related entities what business owners need to know
URL: /transfer-pricing-and-related-entities-what-business-owners-need-to-know

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Why related entity transactions attract IRS scrutiny

Many Bloomington and Indianapolis business owners run more than one legal entity. An optometry practice paired with a separate real estate LLC that owns the building. A dental practice with its own management company. A service business paying a related staffing entity for labor. Whenever money moves between entities you control, the IRS wants confirmation that the price was fair.

Transfer pricing is simply the term for how much one related entity charges another for rent, management services, equipment use, or shared staff. When a practice pays below-market rent to an LLC you also own, or a holding company charges an inflated management fee, the IRS sees a chance for income and deductions to shift between entities in ways that reduce overall tax. That's why these transactions get flagged: they weren't negotiated the way a deal with a stranger would be.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: intercompany-transactions-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing intercompany financial documents at a desk" | query: "business owner reviewing financial documents" -->
## Common situations where transfer pricing rules apply

Related entity transactions show up in ordinary operating decisions, not just complicated corporate structures. If any of these sound familiar, transfer pricing rules likely already apply to your business:

- Management fees paid from an operating practice to a holding company for administrative oversight
- Rent paid by an optometry, dental, or medical practice to a real estate LLC held by the same owner
- A bookkeeper or office manager splitting time across two related businesses without a documented allocation
- Equipment or vehicles shared between a service business and an affiliated entity
- Loans made between commonly owned entities without a market interest rate attached
- A church-affiliated school or daycare sharing staff or facilities with the congregation

None of these arrangements are wrong on their own. The problem starts when the amounts charged don't reflect what an unrelated party would reasonably pay, and there's no record showing how the number was set.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: arms-length-rent-example.jpg | alt: "Accountant explaining fair market rent calculation to a client" | query: "accountant explaining calculation to client" -->
## The arm's length standard explained simply

The standard the IRS applies to related entity pricing has a formal name, but the idea is straightforward: charge what an unrelated party would charge in the same deal.

Say your optometry practice rents its space from an LLC you also own. If a stranger leasing comparable space in Bloomington would pay $28 per square foot, your practice should pay something close to that, not $12 and not $45. The same logic applies to management fees, equipment rental, or staff-sharing arrangements between your entities. The question is never whether related parties can transact with each other. They can, and often should. The question is whether the price would survive a side-by-side comparison to a deal between two unrelated business owners.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: financial-risk-review-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA and client reviewing risk documentation on financial statements" | query: "CPA client reviewing documents meeting" -->
## Risks of getting intercompany pricing wrong

Undocumented or unreasonable pricing between related entities carries real consequences, but they're manageable ones when you know what to watch for:

- The IRS can reclassify income or expenses between entities, changing which one owes tax and how much
- Deductions tied to inflated management fees or rent can be disallowed entirely
- Penalties and interest accrue on any underpayment traced back to the reallocation
- Weak documentation makes an otherwise defensible arrangement look like an audit target

None of this requires a large legal team to fix. It requires consistent documentation and pricing that reflects market terms, set up before a return is filed rather than reconstructed after a notice arrives.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cfo-advisor-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA advisor consulting with business owners around office table" | query: "CPA advisor consulting business owners" -->
## How RootAdvisors helps structure related entity transactions

Jared Hammack, CPA, and the RootAdvisors team work as an outsourced accounting department for optometry practices, dental and medical offices, service businesses, and churches across Bloomington and Indianapolis, many of which operate more than one legal entity. That means related-party pricing gets reviewed as part of ongoing monthly work, not discovered during a scramble at filing season.

Outsourced Accounting keeps the books for each entity clean and consistent, so a management fee or intercompany lease shows up the same way on both sides of the transaction. Business Foundation Services helps set the entity structure and documentation up correctly from the start, whether that's a new real estate LLC or a management company splitting off from an operating practice. Clients pay a fixed monthly fee for this work, not an hourly rate, and get CFO-level insight into whether their intercompany numbers would hold up under review, informed by nearly 40 years of RootAdvisors' work with healthcare providers.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: bloomington-office-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA meeting with local business owner in office setting" | query: "CPA meeting local business owner office" -->
## Getting proactive guidance for your Bloomington or Indianapolis business

If your optometry practice, dental office, medical group, service business, or church operates alongside a related entity, this is worth sorting out before an intercompany transaction lands on a return the IRS decides to look at twice. RootAdvisors works with practice owners and business managers across Bloomington and Indianapolis who need that structure reviewed by someone who already understands healthcare and service-business accounting, not explained from scratch.

A short conversation now, about how your entities charge each other for rent, management, or shared staff, is far less costly than an audit response later. [Schedule a consultation](/contact) with RootAdvisors and get a clear read on where your related entity pricing stands.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: physician-financial-consultation.jpg | alt: "Physician reviewing financial dashboard with an accountant in a clinical office" | query: "physician accountant financial consultation" -->
## Guidance for medical professionals and healthcare providers

Physicians and other healthcare providers deal with reimbursement cycles, coding changes, and compliance requirements that a general-practice CPA firm often treats as an afterthought. Accord Advisors builds bookkeeping and tax strategy around how [medical professionals](/industries/medical-professionals) actually get paid.

- Monthly financials that separate clinical revenue from ancillary income
- Tax planning that accounts for entity structure, retirement contributions, and reimbursement timing
- Direct answers from a CPA who has worked healthcare books for years, not a call center
- Support during payer audits or reimbursement disputes without starting from scratch

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: service-business-owner-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Service business owner reviewing financial dashboard on a laptop with an advisor" | query: "small business owner reviewing financials" -->
## Accounting for service-based businesses

Service businesses, consultants, contractors, agencies, wellness providers, share a common frustration: knowing how last month went before it's too late to act on it. Accord Advisors builds financial dashboards around the metrics that matter for each [service business](/industries/service-businesses), not a generic template pulled from off-the-shelf software.

Whether a business is two years old and still finding its footing, or twenty years in and planning an ownership transition, the numbers need to answer the same question: how did we actually do, and what should change next month? Fixed monthly fees mean owners can call with a quick question without watching the clock, and the secure online platform keeps records available whenever they're needed, not just when the books close.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: church-finance-committee-meeting.jpg | alt: "Church finance committee reviewing budget and contribution reports" | query: "church finance committee meeting" -->
## Financial stewardship for churches and religious organizations

Congregations, boards, and donors expect clear answers about where contributions go, and compliance requirements around payroll, housing allowances, and nonprofit status don't leave much room for guesswork.

Accord Advisors handles the bookkeeping and reporting that keeps [church](/industries/churches) leadership confident in front of a board or a congregation: fund accounting, payroll for pastoral staff, and financial statements that make stewardship visible instead of assumed. Fixed monthly fees keep costs predictable for organizations that run on tight, donor-funded budgets. Churches get a CPA who understands the difference between a for-profit ledger and a stewardship report, and who treats every dollar with the transparency a congregation deserves.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: new-business-owner-planning.jpg | alt: "New business owner and accountant setting up entity and accounting systems" | query: "startup business owner accountant planning" -->
## Business foundation services to get you started right

Starting a business means dozens of decisions before the first invoice goes out: entity structure, bank accounts, bookkeeping systems, payroll setup. Get these wrong early and they're expensive to unwind later. [Business Foundation Services](/services/business-foundation-services) set new and growing businesses up with the structure that lets everything after run smoothly.

- Entity selection and setup guidance, LLC, S-corp, or otherwise
- Chart of accounts and bookkeeping systems built for how the business actually operates
- Payroll and vendor systems ready before day one
- A foundation built to scale as the business grows, not one that needs rebuilding at year three

## Personal income tax planning alongside your business needs

Business owners rarely have simple personal returns. K-1s, quarterly estimates, retirement contributions, and the tax impact of business decisions all flow onto the individual return, and separating that work from the business relationship creates blind spots.

Accord Advisors handles [personal income tax](/services/personal-income-tax) preparation and planning for owners, practice shareholders, and individuals who just want their return done right. Because the same team sees both sides, a decision made in the business, a distribution, an equipment purchase, a change in entity, gets planned for on the personal return before it becomes a surprise in April.

## A clear, simple path to getting started

Deciding to hand off your books, payroll, or tax planning to an outside firm can feel like a big step, especially if you have never worked with an outsourced accounting team before. At Accord Advisors, the process is built to feel more like a conversation than a contract negotiation. Optometry practices, dental offices, medical clinics, service businesses, and churches across Bloomington and Indianapolis come to us because they want clarity, not more paperwork.

Here is what actually happens, step by step, from your first phone call to your first monthly report.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: first-consultation-call.jpg | alt: "CPA speaking with a business owner during an initial consultation call" | query: "advisor phone consultation office" -->
## Your first conversation with us

The first step is a conversation, not a sales pitch. You will talk directly with Jared Hammack, CPA, about what is working in your practice or business and what is not. Maybe your optometry practice manager cannot get a straight answer on monthly performance. Maybe your church board wants better financial oversight. Maybe you are a service business owner tired of surprise invoices from your current accountant.

There is no pressure to sign anything at this stage. The goal is to understand your situation well enough to tell you honestly whether Accord Advisors is the right fit, and if it is, what working together would actually look like.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: reviewing-practice-books.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing financial books and records with a client at a desk" | query: "accountant reviewing financial documents" -->
## How we get to know your business or practice

Once we agree it makes sense to move forward, we take a closer look at your current books, software, and reporting habits. For medical and optometry practices, that includes reimbursement patterns, staffing costs, and the kind of practice management metrics that matter to shareholders. For churches, it means understanding compliance requirements and staffing structure. For service businesses, it means looking at how job costs and cash flow actually move through the year.

This is where nearly 40 years of healthcare industry experience matters. We have seen how optometry and medical practices operate, what breaks down in their books, and what a healthy month actually looks like on paper.

## Setting up your fixed monthly plan

After the review, we build a fixed monthly fee proposal, not an hourly estimate that grows every time you send an email. You will know exactly what you are paying before any work begins, and exactly what is included.

Most engagements combine two of our core services:

- Outsourced Accounting: bookkeeping, reconciliations, and monthly financial reporting handled by our team
- Business Foundation Services: entity structure, payroll setup, and the administrative groundwork every practice or business needs in place
- A written scope so there is no ambiguity about what is covered
- One predictable invoice each month, no hourly surprises

You approve the plan before we do anything else. Nothing moves forward until the numbers make sense to you.

Once the plan is signed, we get you set up on our secure online platform. This is where your financial data lives, and where you will log in to see how your practice or business actually performed last month, not three months from now when your old accountant finally gets around to it.

You get access to dashboards built around what you actually need to see: revenue trends, expense categories, cash position, and the non-financial metrics that matter for your specific industry, whether that is patient volume for a medical practice or giving trends for a church. No spreadsheets emailed back and forth. No guessing where things stand.

### Privacy policy
URL: /privacy-policy

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Our commitment to protecting your information

When you hand over tax documents, payroll records, or practice financials, you're trusting us with details most people never share outside their own household. RootAdvisors takes that trust seriously. Whether you run an optometry practice in Bloomington, manage payroll for a dental office, or handle the books for a church in Avon, the same standard applies: your information stays protected, stays private, and is never used for anything beyond the work you've hired us to do.

This policy explains, in plain language, what information we collect, how we use it, and the steps we take to keep it secure. If anything here raises a question, call us. We'd rather explain it directly than have you guess.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Information we collect from clients

Most of what we collect comes straight from you: tax organizers, W-2s and 1099s, bank and credit card statements, payroll records, and financial documents you upload through our secure online platform. For business clients, that can include profit and loss statements, accounts payable and receivable detail, and entity formation paperwork. For optometry, dental, and medical clients, it may include practice revenue data and billing summaries tied to outsourced accounting work, though never patient charts or clinical records.

We may also receive information from third parties involved in your engagement, such as your bank, payroll processor, or a prior accountant transitioning your files to us. All of it is collected for one reason: to prepare accurate tax returns and deliver the outsourced accounting and Business Foundation Services you've engaged us for.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How we use and share your information

Your information is used to complete the services you've asked for, tax preparation, monthly outsourced accounting, entity setup, or ongoing advisory work. That's the boundary. We don't sell client data, rent mailing lists, or share your financial details with marketers.

Limited sharing does happen in specific, necessary circumstances: with the IRS or Indiana Department of Revenue to file returns, with a bank or lender if you've authorized us to provide documentation for a loan application, or with a successor accountant if you leave our firm and request a file transfer. We may also disclose information when required by law, such as in response to a subpoena. Outside of those situations, what you share with Jared Hammack, CPA, and the RootAdvisors team stays inside the engagement it was collected for.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: data-security-safeguards.jpg | alt: "Accountant securely accessing encrypted financial data on a laptop" | query: "secure data encryption accountant laptop" -->
## Security safeguards for financial and health-related data

Optometry, dental, and medical clients often ask how we handle information that sits close to protected health data, even though we don't process clinical records. The answer is layered safeguards, not a single lock. Our secure online platform uses encryption for document upload and storage, so financial files never travel by unprotected email. Access is limited to team members actively working on your engagement, and internal permissions are reviewed as staff roles change.

Physically, paper documents are stored in locked, access-controlled files and shredded once digitized copies are confirmed. Procedurally, every team member completes confidentiality training before handling client files, and our systems are monitored for unauthorized access attempts. For practices bound by HIPAA on the clinical side, we coordinate so that our accounting processes never create a gap in your own compliance obligations.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Confidentiality for specialized industries

Almost 40 years of working with healthcare providers taught us that confidentiality expectations aren't identical across industries. A church treasurer worries about donor privacy. An optometry practice manager worries about payroll data reaching the wrong staff member. We built our privacy practices around those distinctions.

### Optometry practices
icon: HeartPulse

Practice revenue, staff payroll, and vendor contracts stay confidential from competing practices and unauthorized staff, consistent with the industry expertise behind our optometry accounting work.

### Dental practices
icon: Stethoscope

Financial data tied to associate compensation, equipment financing, and practice transitions is limited to the engagement team handling your books.

### Medical professionals
icon: ClipboardCheck

Reimbursement and revenue data are handled separately from clinical systems, with access restricted to the accountants assigned to your practice.

### Service businesses
icon: Briefcase

Job costing, client contracts, and margin data stay inside your engagement file, never shared with other clients or shown as case studies without permission.

### Churches
icon: Building2

Donor and giving records are treated as confidential financial information, disclosed only to the board members or staff you authorize.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: client-data-rights-review.jpg | alt: "Client and accountant reviewing a document together at a desk" | query: "client accountant reviewing documents desk" -->
## Your rights and choices regarding your data

Under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, you have specific rights over how a financial services firm like ours handles your nonpublic personal information. Here's what that means in practice:

- You can ask what personal or business information we have on file for your engagement.
- You can request that we limit sharing with third parties beyond what's needed to complete your tax return or accounting work.
- You can opt out of nonessential communications, such as general newsletters, at any time.
- You can request a copy of records be transferred to another accountant if you end your engagement with us.
- You can ask questions about this policy before signing an engagement letter, not just after.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: cpa-consultation-handshake.jpg | alt: "CPA and client shaking hands after a consultation meeting" | query: "professional handshake office consultation" -->
## Questions about this privacy policy

If something in this policy isn't clear, or you want to know exactly what happens to your practice's financial data once it's in our system, ask us directly. Clients in Bloomington, Indianapolis, and Avon can reach our team by phone or through the secure client portal, and Jared Hammack, CPA, is available to walk through any concern in plain terms.

Ready to see how an outsourced accounting relationship with real safeguards works? Schedule a consultation and we'll answer every privacy question before you sign anything.

## Understanding these terms

Welcome to the RootAdvisors website. These terms and conditions govern your use of this site and set expectations for how we work together as a CPA firm serving Bloomington and Indianapolis, Indiana. Think of this page as the fine print that keeps things clear, not a wall between you and the help you need.

Nothing here changes the way we treat clients: with straightforward communication and fixed monthly fees instead of surprise hourly bills. If you're an optometry practice manager, a dentist, a physician, a service business owner, or a church administrator exploring outsourced accounting with us, this page simply explains the ground rules for browsing our site and requesting information. The specifics of any actual engagement, whether it's tax preparation, Business Foundation Services, or ongoing outsourced accounting, are always spelled out in a separate signed agreement.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Website use and content

You're welcome to browse rootadvisors.com, read our articles, and reach out through our contact forms. The content on this site, including text, graphics, and resources like our Smart Tips magazine and insights gallery, belongs to RootAdvisors and may not be copied or republished without permission.

Everything published here, from blog posts on tax planning to industry pages for optometry or church accounting, is general information. It reflects nearly 40 years of experience serving healthcare providers, but it is not personalized advice and should never be treated as a substitute for a signed engagement letter. Tax law changes, individual circumstances vary, and Indiana regulations shift year to year. If you read something here and want to know how it applies to your practice or business specifically, that conversation happens once you're an engaged client, guided by Jared Hammack, CPA, and the RootAdvisors team.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Client engagements and service agreements

Browsing this website does not create a client relationship. Actual services, outsourced accounting, personal income tax preparation, and Business Foundation Services, begin only after both parties sign a formal engagement letter that spells out scope, deliverables, timelines, and fees.

We bill on a fixed monthly fee basis rather than by the hour, and that fee structure is confirmed in writing before work begins. Clients access their financials and documents through a secure online platform built to keep sensitive practice and personal data protected, whether you're an optometry practice referred through Acquios, a dental or medical office, a service business, or a church managing staff and donor records.

Each niche we serve, optometry, medical, dental, service businesses, and churches, has its own compliance considerations. Those specifics are addressed inside your engagement letter, not on this general terms page. If you're comparing us to other Indiana accounting firms, ask to see a sample engagement letter before you sign anything.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Confidentiality and data security

Financial data is personal, and for medical, dental, optometry, and church clients, it's often sensitive. Information shared through our secure client portal is protected using industry-standard safeguards, and access is limited to the team members working on your account.

We don't sell or share client financial information with third parties for marketing purposes. That said, no online platform, including ours, can guarantee absolute security against every possible threat. Our engagement letters outline the specific confidentiality obligations and limits of liability tied to the secure portal and any third-party software we use to deliver outsourced accounting, tax, or advisory work. If your organization has particular data handling requirements, whether for HIPAA-adjacent healthcare records or church donor privacy, raise it during onboarding so we can address it directly.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Limitation of liability and disclaimers

Content on this website, including articles on topics like fraud prevention for nonprofits or business valuation timing, is provided for general informational purposes only. It is not professional accounting, tax, or legal advice, and no attorney-client, CPA-client, or advisory relationship is created simply by reading it or submitting a contact form.

RootAdvisors and its team make reasonable efforts to keep information accurate and current, but we don't guarantee that every article or resource reflects the latest Indiana or federal tax rule. To the fullest extent permitted by law, RootAdvisors disclaims liability for decisions made based solely on website content, apart from services delivered under a signed engagement letter. Once you're a client, your engagement letter, not this page, governs the scope of our responsibility.

## Governing law and updates to these terms

These terms are governed by the laws of the State of Indiana, without regard to conflict-of-law principles. As a firm based in Bloomington and serving clients throughout the Indianapolis area, we operate under Indiana professional accounting standards and expect the same of the agreements we sign with clients.

We may update this page occasionally to reflect changes in our services, technology, or legal requirements. When we do, the revised date will be noted and the updated terms will apply going forward. We'd encourage you to check back periodically, particularly if you're a returning client using our secure portal or reviewing service details before an engagement renewal.

## Questions about these terms

Legal language should never leave you more confused than when you started. If anything on this page raises a question, about how our fixed monthly fees work, how the secure portal protects your practice's data, or what a signed engagement letter with RootAdvisors actually looks like, we're glad to walk through it.

Reach out anytime, or schedule a consultation and we'll answer your questions directly, in plain language, before you commit to anything.
